questions.skill: Describe a distribution using the resource: general pattern, specific evidence, anomaly

stimulus.label: Figure 1
stimulus.caption: A world map showing the tracks of tropical storms over a 20-year period. Storm tracks are concentrated between about 5° and 30° north and south of the Equator. They start over oceans and move westwards, often curving away from the Equator. Many tracks are shown in the western Pacific, the Caribbean and the Bay of Bengal. There are no tracks in the South Atlantic or directly on the Equator.

questions.prompt: Using Figure 1, describe the distribution of tropical storms.

answers.text: Tropical storms are found in the tropics, mostly between 5° and 30° north and south of the Equator. They form over oceans, for example the western Pacific and the Caribbean Sea, and generally move westwards. There are very few storms directly on the Equator, and none in the South Atlantic Ocean.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): a clear description of the overall pattern (tropics), specific evidence from the map (latitudes, named oceans), the direction of movement, and anomalies (none on the Equator or in the South Atlantic). It describes and never explains.

answers.text: Tropical storms are found near the Equator in hot areas, such as the Caribbean. They are found over the sea.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a basic pattern with one named example. It needs more precise use of the map: latitudes, more named areas, and where storms are absent.

answers.text: Tropical storms form over warm oceans where the sea is above 27 °C. They need the Coriolis effect to spin, which is why they don't form on the Equator. They lose energy when they reach land, because they are no longer over warm water to feed them. They are called hurricanes, cyclones or typhoons depending on where they form.
answers.explanation: Mostly explanation, which the command word 'describe' does not ask for. Only the general idea that storms form over oceans (the pattern) can be credited; the reasons, and the different names for storms, earn nothing here. Save causes for an 'explain' or 'suggest why' question.

answers.text: Tropical storms are very dangerous. They cause lots of damage and kill many people, like Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines in 2013.
answers.explanation: Zero. This is about the effects of storms, not their distribution (where they are found). It doesn't use Figure 1 at all.

questions.tip: For 'describe the distribution', use the acronym G-E-A: General pattern, Evidence (latitudes, places, numbers from the resource), and Anomalies (exceptions).

questions.paper: Paper 1: Living with the physical environment
questions.skill: Develop each point into a chain of reasoning ('this means that…')
questions.prompt: Explain why the effects of earthquakes are often greater in low-income countries (LICs) than in high-income countries (HICs).

answers.text: In LICs many buildings are not earthquake-resistant because of the cost, so more collapse, causing more deaths. LICs also have fewer emergency services and hospitals, which means injured people are not rescued or treated quickly, so more die after the earthquake.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): two points, each developed into a clear chain of reasoning (cause, then consequence, then effect on deaths or damage). The connectives 'so', 'which leads to' and 'which means' show the development examiners reward.

answers.text: LICs have poorer quality buildings, which are more likely to collapse in an earthquake and kill people. They also have fewer hospitals.
answers.explanation: Level 2, low (3 marks): the first point is developed well, but the second is left undeveloped. Add a 'which means…' to every point: fewer hospitals, which means injured people aren't treated and more die.

answers.text: They are poorer, they have worse buildings, fewer hospitals, less money for aid and less education about earthquakes.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a list of relevant ideas, but none is explained. In a 4-mark 'explain' question, two developed points beat five undeveloped ones.

answers.text: Earthquakes happen at plate boundaries, and some of the biggest earthquakes have happened in HICs such as Japan and the USA. The effects are often greater in LICs because LICs are poor. HICs are rich countries and LICs are poor countries, which is the main difference between them, so LICs can't cope as well.
answers.explanation: Level 1, low: a valid basic idea (LICs are poor), but it never explains how being poor makes the effects greater. The rest defines HICs and LICs and says where earthquakes happen, which earns nothing. One mark at most.

questions.tip: Use 'point, then develop': make a point, then add 'this means that…' and a consequence. Two well-developed points are enough for 4 marks.

questions.paper: Paper 1: Living with the physical environment
questions.skill: Use a named example with place-specific detail and reach a justified conclusion
questions.prompt:
'The benefits of flood management schemes outweigh the costs.'

Using an example of a flood management scheme in the UK, to what extent do you agree with this statement?

answers.text:
I largely agree, using the example of the Banbury flood scheme on the River Cherwell, completed in 2012. It cost around £18.5 million, but it protects over 400 homes and 70 businesses that had flooded badly in 1998 and 2007. A 2.9 km earth embankment created a flood storage area that holds back water and releases it slowly, and the main A361 road was raised so it stays open during floods. The scheme also created a new wetland habitat, an environmental benefit.

However, there were costs. The scheme was expensive, and the storage area floods farmland, affecting farmers. The embankment also changed the look of the floodplain.

Overall, the benefits outweigh the costs, because a single major flood can cause damage costing more than the scheme itself (the 1998 flood alone caused around £12.5 million of damage in Banbury), and it also reduces stress and insurance costs for residents.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (7–9 marks): a thorough evaluation using a named UK scheme with place-specific detail (cost, dates, homes protected, features). It weighs social, economic and environmental benefits against costs and reaches a justified conclusion that directly answers 'to what extent'.

answers.text:
The Banbury flood scheme cost £18.5 million. It protects hundreds of homes and businesses from flooding. It includes an embankment to create a flood storage area, and the A361 road was raised. There is also a new wildlife habitat.

However, it was very expensive and farmland is used to store flood water.
answers.explanation: Level 2, top (4–6 marks): a named example with good specific detail and both benefits and costs, but no conclusion. Without a judgement it can't reach Level 3, however good the detail.

answers.text: I agree that the benefits outweigh the costs. Flood management schemes like dams, embankments and flood walls stop houses from flooding, which saves money and stops people getting hurt. They can be expensive and look ugly, but they are worth it because floods can be very destructive.
answers.explanation: Level 2, low: it has a judgement and some balance, but no named example, even though the question asks for one. Generic answers cap your mark. Learn three or four facts about your case study.

answers.text: Flooding happens when a river bursts its banks and water spreads onto the floodplain. It is caused by heavy rainfall, snowmelt and urbanisation, as impermeable surfaces mean water runs off quickly into the river. Deforestation also increases flood risk because fewer trees intercept the rain. Floods can damage homes and businesses and even kill people, so they are a serious hazard.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–3 marks): accurate but irrelevant. It explains the causes and effects of flooding, not whether management schemes are worth it, and never names a scheme. Only a small amount of credit is given for relevant understanding.

questions.tip: About 12 minutes. Name your example in the first line, use at least three specific facts, cover both sides, and finish with 'Overall, I agree to a large extent because…'. Up to 3 extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

questions.skill: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100, with working shown
questions.prompt:
Using Figure 2, calculate the percentage increase in the population of Lagos between 1990 and 2020.

Show your working.

answers.explanation: Full marks: correct method (change ÷ original × 100) and the correct answer with a % sign.
One mark for finding the change correctly, but it was divided by the new value instead of the original. Percentage change is always compared with the starting value.

answers.text:
Population in 1990 = 4.8 million
Population in 2020 = 14.4 million
14.4 ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 300%
The population increased by 300%.
answers.explanation: Zero. This shows the 2020 population as a percentage of the 1990 population, not the increase. A population that triples has increased by 200%, not 300%. Copying the data out neatly doesn't earn marks on its own.

questions.tip: Skills questions appear on every paper and are quick marks. Learn: % change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Show each step and include the unit.

questions.skill: Eastings first ('along the corridor'), then northings ('up the stairs')
questions.prompt:
On an Ordnance Survey map, a church is in grid square 4317.
It is three-tenths of the way across the square from the western edge, and six-tenths of the way up from the southern edge.

Give the six-figure grid reference of the church.

answers.explanation: Full marks: easting 43 plus 3 tenths (433), then northing 17 plus 6 tenths (176).

answers.text:
Grid square 4317
(easting 43, northing 17)
answers.explanation: One mark at most: this is the four-figure reference for the square. The question asks for six figures, which pinpoint the church within the square. Labelling the easting and northing is good practice, but the answer still stops at four figures.
Zero: the northing has been given first. Always read along the corridor (eastings) before going up the stairs (northings).

questions.tip: Along the corridor, then up the stairs. For six figures, estimate tenths across the square, then tenths up it.

questions.skill: Put the data in order before finding the median; the range is a single value
questions.prompt:
A student measured river velocity at five sites (m/s):

0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.8, 0.4

Calculate the range and the median.

answers.explanation: Full marks: the range as the difference between the highest and lowest values (1), and the median found after ordering the data (1).

answers.text:
Range = 0.8 − 0.2 = 0.6 m/s
Median = 0.2 m/s (the middle number in the list)
answers.explanation: One mark for the range. The median is the middle value after putting the data in order; here the middle of the unordered list was used.

answers.text:
Range = 0.2 to 0.8 m/s
Median = 0.44 m/s (the average)
answers.explanation: Zero. The range is one number (the difference), not two end points, and 0.44 is the mean, not the median.

questions.tip: Median: order the data first. Range: highest minus lowest, as one number with units. Mean: add up and divide.

questions.skill: Describe the overall trend, use data with units, and note changes in the rate

stimulus.label: Figure 1
stimulus.caption: Average atmospheric CO₂ concentration measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii.

questions.prompt: Using Figure 1, describe the changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration between 1960 and 2020.

answers.text: It rose steadily, from about 317 ppm in 1960 to about 414 ppm in 2020, and the rise sped up: +22 ppm from 1960 to 1980 but +44 ppm from 2000 to 2020.
answers.explanation: Full marks: the overall trend (1), data with units (1), and the change in the rate of increase (1).

answers.text: Looking at Figure 1, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere changed a lot between 1960 and 2020. CO₂ went up from 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020, which is a big change.
answers.explanation: Two marks: the trend with data. Look for a third point: here, the increase is accelerating. 'Changed a lot' and 'a big change' restate the question rather than adding a point.

answers.text: It went up.
answers.explanation: One mark for the basic trend, but 'describe' questions using a figure expect specific data.

answers.text: Carbon dioxide increased because people burn more fossil fuels and cut down rainforests.
answers.explanation: Zero. This explains rather than describes, and uses no data from the figure.

questions.tip: Trend → data (with units and years) → anomaly or change in rate. Don't explain unless asked.

questions.skill: Use evidence from the photo and link each feature to flood risk

stimulus.label: Figure 2
stimulus.caption: [Photograph: a town centre on flat, low-lying land beside a river. Buildings, car parks and roads cover most of the ground right up to the river bank. There are few trees or open green spaces.]

questions.prompt:
Figure 2 shows part of a town centre next to a river.

Suggest two reasons why this area may be at risk of flooding.

answers.text: Most of the ground is covered by concrete, tarmac and roofs, which are impermeable, so rainwater runs off quickly into drains and the river instead of soaking in. The buildings are also built right up to the river on low, flat land, so if the river overtops its banks there is nowhere for the water to go except into the buildings.
answers.explanation: Full marks: two reasons, each based on evidence visible in the photo and developed into a clear link to flood risk.

answers.text: There are lots of roads and buildings. It is near the river.
answers.explanation: Two marks: two relevant features, but neither is explained. Add 'which means…' to link each one to flooding.

answers.text: Figure 2 shows a town centre next to a river, which could flood. It might rain a lot, and if there is a lot of rain the river could flood the town.
answers.explanation: One mark at most: rain is relevant everywhere, so this isn't a reason based on the photo. Describing the photo in general terms ('a town centre next to a river') just repeats the question.

questions.tip: 'Suggest' + photo: point to something you can see, then explain how it increases the risk.

questions.skill: Give an advantage and a disadvantage, each explained in the context of your enquiry
questions.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a questionnaire to collect data in a human geography enquiry.

answers.text: Advantage: it records people's opinions directly (e.g. how safe residents feel after regeneration), which can't be measured another way. Disadvantage: people may answer dishonestly or misunderstand a question, so the data may be unreliable.
answers.explanation: Full marks: an advantage and a disadvantage, each explained and linked to the reliability or usefulness of the data.

answers.text:
Advantage: you can get people's opinions, which is useful in a human geography enquiry and is one of the main advantages of questionnaires.
Disadvantage: people might lie, which is a disadvantage of using a questionnaire because it is a problem.
answers.explanation: Two marks: valid points, but neither is explained. Develop each with 'because' or 'which means'. The 'which…' phrases only repeat the question ('useful', 'a disadvantage', 'a problem'), so they don't count as explanation.

answers.text: It is easy to do.
answers.explanation: One mark at most: a vague advantage and no disadvantage.

questions.tip: Fieldwork questions reward reasons: why is this useful, and how does it affect the reliability or accuracy of the results?

questions.skill: 'Justify' means give reasons why your choice was appropriate
questions.prompt: Justify the sampling method you used to choose sites for your river fieldwork.

answers.text: Systematic sampling: a site every 200 m along the river. This gave an even spread from upstream to downstream, so we could see how the channel changed with distance, and it avoided bias because we couldn't just pick the easiest spots.
answers.explanation: Full marks: the method named and described (1), with two reasons why it suited this enquiry (2).

answers.text: We used systematic sampling every 200 m.
answers.explanation: One mark for naming and describing the method, but 'justify' needs reasons why it was a good choice.

answers.text: We went to the river on a sunny day in June and worked in groups of four. At each site we measured the width with a tape measure, the depth with a metre ruler and the velocity using a float and a stopwatch, and we recorded everything on a data sheet.
answers.explanation: Zero. This describes the day and what was measured in some detail, but not how the sites were chosen or why. Read the question: it is only about sampling.

questions.tip: Justify = 'I chose X because…'. Link the reason to your enquiry question, and to reducing bias or improving reliability.

questions.skill: Link the shape of the pyramid to birth rate, death rate or migration
questions.prompt:
A population pyramid for Country A has a very wide base and narrows quickly towards the top.

Suggest one reason why the pyramid has this shape.

answers.text: Country A probably has a high birth rate, perhaps because of limited access to contraception or children being needed to work on farms, which makes the base wide. It narrows quickly because life expectancy is low, so few people live to old age.
answers.explanation: Full marks: a valid reason (1) developed with an explanation of how it produces the shape (1).

answers.text: It has a high birth rate.
answers.explanation: One mark: correct, but not developed. Explain why, or link it to the shape.

answers.text: Because it is a big country with lots of people.
answers.explanation: Zero. The size of the population doesn't determine the shape of the pyramid.

questions.tip: Wide base = high birth rate. Narrow top = low life expectancy. Bulges = migration or baby booms.

questions.skill: Use continents, compass directions, lines of latitude and neighbouring places
questions.prompt: Using an atlas map of South America, describe the location of Brazil.

answers.text: Eastern South America, with a long Atlantic coastline. The Equator crosses the north and the Tropic of Capricorn the south. It borders most South American countries, including Argentina to the south-west and Colombia to the north-west.
answers.explanation: Full marks: continent and position within it (1), a line of latitude (1), and neighbouring countries or oceans with compass directions (1).

answers.text: Brazil is in South America, on the east coast next to the Atlantic Ocean.
answers.explanation: Two marks: good, but add a line of latitude or neighbouring countries for the third mark.

answers.text: Brazil is in South America.
answers.explanation: One mark: correct, but too basic for 3 marks.

answers.text: Brazil is a very large country and it is hot, with a tropical climate. It has the Amazon rainforest and the Amazon River, and its capital is Brasília. Its biggest cities are São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. It is also famous for football and carnival.
answers.explanation: Zero. This describes Brazil's climate, features and cities, not its location (where it is). Location answers use the continent, lines of latitude, oceans and neighbouring countries.

questions.tip: Location = where it is: continent, compass position, lines of latitude, oceans, neighbours. Features and climate are not location.

questions.paper: Paper 2: Challenges in the human environment
questions.skill: Use a named example with specific detail, and link each change to quality of life
questions.prompt: Using an example, explain how urban regeneration can improve quality of life.

answers.text: The regeneration of Stratford, East London, for the 2012 Olympics improved quality of life. The athletes' village became East Village, providing thousands of new homes, some affordable, for people from overcrowded housing. Westfield Stratford City created thousands of jobs, raising incomes in a deprived borough. Better transport links help residents reach jobs across London, and the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park provides green space for leisure and health. However, rising house prices have priced some original residents out.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks): a named example with specific detail, several ways quality of life improved (housing, jobs, transport, green space), each clearly explained, and some balance.

answers.text: In Stratford, London, the Olympic Park was built. It gave people new houses and jobs, and there is a big shopping centre. There are also parks, which make it nicer to live there.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): a named example with relevant changes, but explanations of how quality of life improved are brief and the detail is limited.

answers.text: Urban regeneration is when an old, run-down area of a city is improved. This can improve quality of life in lots of ways. Regeneration can make areas nicer, with new houses and shops, and there will be fewer crimes because the area is looked after. There will be more jobs, so people will have more money, and new parks and green spaces make people healthier and happier. Transport can also be improved, with new roads and train stations. All of these things make it a much better place to live, which improves quality of life for the people who live there.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): relevant general points, but no named example, which caps the mark however many points are made. 'Using an example' means a real place with specific detail.

answers.text: Urban regeneration is when an old area is improved. It happens in lots of cities in the UK, especially in areas where old industries such as docks and factories have closed down and the buildings are empty.
answers.explanation: Level 1, low: a definition and some background on where regeneration happens, with no explanation of quality of life.

questions.tip: Name your example in the first sentence. Give 2–3 specific changes, and for each say how it improved people's lives.

questions.paper: Paper 1: Living with the physical environment
questions.skill: Weigh benefits against limits using an example, then reach a justified judgement
questions.prompt:
'Ecotourism is the best way to manage tropical rainforests sustainably.'

To what extent do you agree with this statement?

answers.text:
I agree to a large extent. In Costa Rica, around a quarter of the land is protected in national parks and reserves, and ecotourism brings in income that gives local people and the government a reason to keep forests standing rather than cut them down. Small-scale lodges employ local guides, so communities benefit directly, and visitor numbers can be limited to reduce damage.

However, ecotourism has limits. It only works in accessible, attractive areas, it relies on tourists flying long distances, which adds to climate change, and income can fall suddenly, as it did during the pandemic. Other strategies, such as international debt-for-nature swaps, selective logging and national protection laws, are also needed.

Overall, ecotourism is one of the best ways because it makes conservation profitable for local people, but it is most sustainable when combined with legal protection.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (7–9 marks): a thorough evaluation using a named example with specific detail, considering advantages, limits and alternatives, and reaching a clear, justified conclusion. Up to 3 more marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

answers.text: Ecotourism is sustainable because it brings money into the area without destroying the rainforest. For example, in Costa Rica tourists come to see wildlife, and local people get jobs as guides. However, tourists travel by plane, which causes pollution. There are other ways to manage rainforests, like selective logging.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (4–6 marks): a named example and some balance, but the detail is limited and there's no clear judgement about 'to what extent'.

answers.text: I agree because ecotourism doesn't damage the rainforest and it makes money for people.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–3 marks): a simple, one-sided opinion with no example.

answers.text: Tropical rainforests have lots of biodiversity and are being cut down for farming and logging.
answers.explanation: Level 1, low: background knowledge that doesn't address the statement.

questions.tip: About 12 minutes. For: example and detail. Against: limits and alternatives. Then 'Overall, I agree to a large extent because…'. Leave time to check your spelling, punctuation and grammar.

questions.skill: 'Assess' means weigh the importance of factors and reach a judgement
questions.prompt: Assess the importance of physical factors in causing river flooding.

answers.text:
Physical factors are often the main trigger. Intense or prolonged rainfall matters most because it supplies the water; if the ground is saturated, infiltration stops and surface runoff rises rapidly. Impermeable rock such as clay, steep slopes and a small, circular basin also shorten the lag time.

However, human factors can be just as important: urbanisation creates impermeable surfaces and deforestation reduces interception, both increasing runoff.

Overall, physical factors, especially intense rainfall, usually cause the flood, but how serious it is depends on human land use.
answers.explanation: Top level (6–8 marks): several physical factors explained, weighed against human factors, with a clear, supported judgement about their relative importance.

answers.text: Heavy rainfall is an important physical factor because it provides lots of water. If the ground is saturated the water can't soak in and runs off into the river. Steep slopes make water reach the river quickly. Human factors like urbanisation also cause flooding because concrete is impermeable.
answers.explanation: Middle level (3–5 marks), high: good explanation of physical factors and a human counter-point, but there is no judgement about their relative importance.

answers.text: Rain, steep slopes and impermeable rock cause flooding. Building towns also causes flooding.
answers.explanation: Lower middle: relevant factors listed, but none is explained.

answers.text: Flooding is when a river bursts its banks and water spreads out over the land around it, which is called the floodplain. Floods can be very dangerous. They can damage houses, shops and roads, and people may have to be evacuated from their homes. Farmland can be covered in water, so crops are ruined, and electricity and water supplies can be cut off. It can cost millions of pounds to repair the damage afterwards, and insurance becomes more expensive. In some countries, floods kill a lot of people. In the UK there have been many serious floods in recent years, for example in Cumbria and Somerset.
answers.explanation: Level 1: a definition followed by the effects of flooding, which the question doesn't ask about. It never assesses any physical factor, so the extra length earns nothing.

questions.tip: 'Assess': explain the factors, compare their importance, and finish with a judgement ('the most important factor is… because…').

questions.skill: One reason, developed into a two-step explanation
questions.prompt: Explain one reason why tropical storms weaken when they reach land.

answers.text: Over land the storm is cut off from the warm, moist air rising off the ocean, which is its energy source, so it weakens.
answers.explanation: Full marks: the reason (loss of the warm ocean energy supply) (1), developed to explain how this weakens the storm (1).

answers.text: Tropical storms weaken when they reach land because there is no warm sea there, and tropical storms need a warm sea to keep going.
answers.explanation: One mark for the idea, but it isn't developed. Explain why the warm sea matters (it supplies the heat and moisture). Saying storms 'need a warm sea' repeats the idea without saying what the sea supplies.

answers.text: Because the land stops the wind, as there are lots of buildings and hills in the way.
answers.explanation: Zero. Friction does slow the winds a little, but this isn't explained, and the main reason is the loss of the ocean energy supply.

questions.tip: Two-mark 'explain one' questions: make one point, then develop it with 'so' or 'which means'. Don't list several reasons.
